title: GPU eviction policy experimentation journal
body:
Purpose:
This is a working journal for controlled experiments around GPU eviction and soft-ECC-triggered proactive eviction. Goal: reduce frequency of downstream driver panics/kernel-context-loss by evicting noisy/at-risk workloads early, without regressing throughput or increasing request tail-latency beyond SLOs.

Context / why now:
- Over the last 6 months we've seen bursts of correctable ECC errors that precede a small but measurable fraction of driver hangs and full node kernel panics.
- NVLink negotiation timeouts sometimes correlate with degraded thermal transients and ECC bursts on adjacent GPUs.
- Existing eviction is primarily eviction-by-oom/sigkill and periodic garbage collection; there is no heuristic that uses hardware-correctable-errors or NVLink error counters as first-class signals.
- On-call has repeatedly asked for a graduated, reversible strategy so we can avoid rushy mass reboots.

Observed signal candidates (what we can read cheaply):
- nvidia-smi --query-gpu=memory.used,memory.total,utilization.gpu,temperature.gpu,ecc.errors.corrected.volatile --format=csv
- sysfs counters: /sys/class/drm/card*/device/ (link_status, ecc_stats...)
- dmesg/journalctl kernel logs: nvlink negotiation warnings, NV error messages, GPU reset sequences
- Prometheus metrics already in exporters: gpu_ecc_correctable_total (per card) + gpu_nvlink_errors_total
- latency percentiles from request traces (p50/p95/p99) and eviction counts per host

Hypotheses (ranked):
1) Short-lived spikes in correctable ECC rate on a single card often precede a driver-context loss on that card within 1-6 minutes. Proactive eviction of the process using most memory on that card will reduce hard resets. (high priority)
2) NVLink negotiation flaps are more likely when adjacent-card ECC rates are high; isolating traffic (prevent placing latency-sensitive jobs across affected NVLink pairs) reduces inter-GPU escalation. (medium priority)
3) Aggressive eviction on low-util hosts hurts overall throughput as cold-cache misses increase; need backoff windows and grace periods to avoid oscillation. (high priority)

Experiment design (canary -> rollout):
Phase A: passive monitoring (1 week)
- Deploy exporter changes to capture per-GPU correctable-ecc-rate per minute (new metric: gpu_ecc_correctable_per_minute), and NVLink negotiation error spikes.
- Add dashboard panel and alert-only rules: alert when gpu_ecc_correctable_per_minute > 10 for 3 consecutive minutes. No automated action. Collect historical correlation with driver-reset events.

Phase B: simulated eviction (2 weeks)
- Implement a dry-run eviction controller that selects candidate PIDs but only logs actions (no SIGKILL). Controller will: identify the top memory-using PID on the card, note container id, pod name, stack, and simulate eviction score.
- Add an 'eviction_score' formula combining: ECC-rate (weight 0.6), nvlink-err-rate (0.2), temperature delta (0.1), memory pressure (0.1).
- Run on 5% of hosts (canary pool) with mixed workloads. Collect metrics: simulated_evictions, simulated_eviction_impact_on_latency, pre/post DDR cache hit ratio.

Phase C: controlled eviction (4 weeks)
- If dry-run correlation looks promising, enable actual eviction on canary pool with strict rollback: send SIGTERM to target process, allow 30s graceful shutdown, escalate to SIGKILL at 90s. Record time-to-restart and failed-requests.
- Eviction policy parameters (initial):
  - trigger: gpu_ecc_correctable_per_minute >= 20 sustained for 2 minutes on a single GPU
  - OR: gpu_nvlink_errors_per_minute >= 5 sustained 2 minutes for an NVLink pair
  - grace_window: 60s (before forcing kill)
  - cooldown: 15 minutes for that host after an eviction (do not evict again unless metric recovers)
- Runbook: automated eviction should notify #sre-gpu-alerts with host/pid/gpu-id and link to logs. On-call to check within 10 minutes and mark whether eviction likely prevented escalation.

Success criteria / metrics to watch:
- Primary safety metric: reduction in driver-reset frequency per host (target: 40% reduction vs baseline)
- Application-level: change in p95 request latency across affected services (target: p95 regression <= 5%)
- Throughput: tokens/sec on dedicated pools (target: regression <= 3%)
- False positive rate: fraction of evictions where process had no subsequent hardware errors in past 10 min (target: <= 20%)
- Host churn: number of node reboots/week (should decrease)

Rollback criteria:
- Any sustained p95 latency increase >10% for >30m in canary pool
- Any increase in failed requests >2x baseline for >15m
- Host CPU steal or increased preemption implying eviction thrashing
- >5% of evicted containers require manual intervention to come back healthy

Operational runbook draft (for on-call):
- Alert: "gpu-ecc-proactive-eviction-fired" - contains host, gpu-id, eviction_score, pid/container
- Immediate steps: check Prometheus graph for gpu_ecc_correctable_per_minute and nvlink errors for 30m window; run:
  - ssh ops@<host> sudo journalctl -u kubelet -n 200 | grep -i nvidia
  - ssh ops@<host> sudo nvidia-smi --query-gpu=index,name,uuid,memory.used,ecc.errors.corrected.volatile --format=csv
  - export RAW_ECC=$(ssh ops@<host> sudo cat /sys/class/drm/card${GPU}/device/ecc_correctable_count || echo 0)
- If eviction reduced error progression (no new driver resets in 10m), mark incident as mitigated and set a follow-up ticket to analyze logs.
- If eviction failed and a driver reset/hang still occurs, escalate to infra on-call and collect core dump per reset procedure.

Edge cases & known risks:
- Evicting long-running, stateful model processes (serving large KV caches) loses warm cache and can multiply downstream latency. Mitigation: detect if process is tagged 'stateful' and increase trigger thresholds by 3x or prefer soft isolation (move traffic off-node) instead of kill.
- Oscillation: if eviction increases cold start latency, we may induce further errors under heavy load. Mitigation: cooldown windows, cohort-based eviction (limit to 1 eviction per 15m per rack).
- Container orchestration killers: kubelet eviction and our controller might conflict; ensure leader election and coordinate using annotation 'redwood.io/eviction-controller-v1' to avoid double-eviction.

Data collection checklist (what to keep for postmortem):
- per-gpu ECC time-series (1m cadence) 30m before to 60m after each eviction
- kernel logs (dmesg + journalctl) for 1h pre/post
- container logs for target PID
- kube events and pod restart counts for 24h window
- nvlink counters for neighbor GPUs

Open questions / TODOs (short-term):
- What threshold of corrected ECCs is actually meaningful on our Ampere-3 fleet? (need cross-team test with hardware)
- Can firmware retry parameters be tuned remotely to reduce NVLink negotiation flaps? (ask HW partner)
- Add trace context to eviction notifications so SREs can quickly map requests to user-facing traces (Zipkin/OTel link).
- Full integration test: simulate ECC bursts in lab to validate sensitivity and false positive rate.

Notes from recent on-call runs (raw):
- 2027-05-28 03:12 UTC: host rwd-gpu-pool-23 had ecc spike on GPU2 (18/min for 4m), controller logged a simulated eviction; 2m later nvlink negotiation warnings in dmesg, driver reset 6m after initial spike. Dry-run would have flagged but not prevented.
- 2027-06-03 11:20 UTC: observed back-to-back correctable bursts across three GPUs on a host. Likely thermal transient from aggressive fan policy change. Evicting only the top process might not be enough; consider host-level light-drain policy if multi-card spikes detected.

Immediate next steps (this week):
- instrument exporter (Eleni) and dashboard (Miguel) for new ecc_per_min metric (due 2027-06-14)
- implement dry-run controller (Samir) targeting 5% canary hosts (due 2027-06-18)
- schedule lab fault injection session with Applied ML (request via infra-tasks ticket INF-4160)
- draft PR with leader-election/annotation coordination to avoid kubelet conflict (owner: Aisha)

Longer-term (quarter):
- integrate eviction decisions with rollout policies in console so Dedicated customers can opt into "proactive hardware protection" mode.
- evaluate firmware/driver updates in collaboration with hardware partners to reduce correctable-to-uncorrectable escalation window.

Appendix: useful commands and exporters
- quick ECC snapshot: nvidia-smi --query-gpu=index,name,ecc.errors.corrected.volatile --format=csv
- continuous ECC tail watch: while true; do nvidia-smi --query-gpu=index,ecc.errors.corrected.volatile --format=csv; sleep 60; done
- read sysfs counter (card 0 example): sudo cat /sys/class/drm/card0/device/ecc_correctable_count
- grep nvlink in kernel logs: sudo journalctl -k | grep -i nvlink

Comments/notes: this is a working doc; keep it iterative. When we have initial dry-run correlations we will convert to a lightweight runbook and a consolidated postmortem template.
